doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Why the flute: cousins, father doubling, holding the instrument
summary: He started on alto, returned to flute; cousins played flute in bands, his father doubled on many instruments, and the flute embouchure resembles the trumpet's.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: My cousins played flute and I started actually on the alto saxophone, as you know my father is a saxophonist. And for some strange reason I never really had a connection with the alto saxophone. But I started on the flute first, switched to the alto, went back to the flute and there was some kind of connection that I actually made with the instrument the second time around. The interesting thing about the flute is it’s a really tough instrument in terms of holding it. And I tell that to a lot of young flutists like who want to start playing the flute like when they’re in the second or third grade, don’t start, start on piccolo. Because you have a tendency to grab the horn because it’s big. It doesn’t look big physically but when you think about it, it’s really humongous. And so when I go around and I see a lot of young students I can tell, yeah, you started really early because you’re grabbing the horn — you’re not holding the horn, because you’re struggling with it. And somebody, you might remember this, came up with the idea of actually curving it around to shorten it.

All right, and the reason why is because you see you go from here to here. The position. And somebody figured that out. And so basically I had a lot of cousins who were great flutists. I mean flute, at that time, was an instrument that fit in the marching band, there really wasn’t a lot of like youth orchestras around during that time so basically when you played the flute you were going to play in a band, a marching band, concert band. And they really excelled at playing the instrument and I learned a lot from them. And my father was very supportive, because he played a little flute at the time because he was always — I mean I remember him with the bassoon, the saxophones, the oboe, the flute. Because he would say well you never know what you have to play if somebody comes in town with a show, you know, to have to double on all these instruments. And so consequently a lot of saxophone players who were doublers were also flutists in a way.

And they always talk about it being very difficult. Because in actuality the flute is closer to the trumpet than the saxophone in terms of the embouchure if you think about it. You know because you have that open kind of focused, centered kind of an embouchure that you have to deal with. And in fact I knew of a couple of trumpet players who actually doubled on flute and trumpet which I thought was really interesting.
